problems: Battles 1-10 all feel the same: one procedurally recoloured blob monster with a bigger HP bar and a turn counter. Battle 10 is a 'BOSS' that is just the same blob with horns and 119 HP, with no new attack pattern, arena or set piece. Abilities (stone, poison, rage...) come from a random roll, so they are not introduced on purpose. There are only 3 backgrounds across 30 battles.

Each swap waits for the whole cascade, the orb flight, the damage numbers and the monster's turn before you can move again (about 1.5-2s of dead time per move). On the phone my touch bot only got 8 swipes into a 40-poll window. The rhythm is wait-swipe-wait, not a fast combo rush. The cascade combos need a much bigger payoff (pitch-rising chain sound, slow-mo, screen-filling hit).

The VICTORY screen only shows stars, +gold and +XP. There is no tease of the next monster or region and no count-up. The phone map has the shared gb.js settings tab sitting on top of the HERO button. Upgrades/relics are plain DOM lists, and nothing surprising happens during a fight (no monster reactions, critters or golden runes).
rune-match.notes: Puzzle Quest-style match-3: swipe runes on an 8x8 board, and each colour becomes a sword, fire, ice, heal or shield spell against one monster per wave. It works on touch and mouse and the art is clean, but it is a slow, samey turn loop with 30 numbered battles.

problems: The curve is still jagged, and the spikes land on the level that brings in a new idea instead of on the bosses. Game-time bot, 8 runs per cell, 4% typos: at 10 WPM 1-1 to 1-4 are 8/8, then 1-5 (the first fork) is 0/8, and 1-6 (boss) jumps back to 7/8. At 18 WPM, 2-4 (first double gate) is 2/8, 3-3 is 3/8 and 3-4 is 0/8, but the 3-6 boss is 8/8. At 30 WPM, 4-2 to 4-4 are 4/8, 2/8 and 3/8, but the 4-6 boss is 8/8. Show each new idea safely first (no chase pressure on the first fork or double gate) and make the bosses the real peak.

World 5 is a cliff, not a climb. A 30 WPM bot is 8/8 on the 4-6 boss, then 0/8 on every level from 5-2 to 5-6. A 50 WPM bot wins 0/4 on 5-2, 1/4 on 5-3 and 5-4, and 0/4 on 5-5 and 5-6, so the last world needs about 70 WPM. 5-2 (target 34 WPM) is harder than 5-3 (target 50) because 35-character phrase gates plus the rubber band leave no room. Ramp world 5 in from about 35 WPM and cap the phrase length on the early levels there.

The chase still doesn't feel close most of the time, and when it is close it feels unfair. Over winning runs, the average gap to Trace is 9-14 m at 18-30 WPM in worlds 1-3 (about 6-8 m only for a 30 WPM player in world 1). Most losses come 5-7 seconds into the level, at the very first gate, because the rubber band assumes you type at the level's target speed and pulls Trace up before you've finished one word. Have the rubber band hold Trace about 4-6 m back based on how fast you actually type, and give a grace period on the first word.

The 'Trace gets slower next try!' assist barely works, so a stuck kid stays stuck. With 4 recorded fails (the maximum assist), an 18 WPM bot is still 1/4 on 2-4 and 0/4 on 3-4, and a 10 WPM bot is still 0/4 on 2-4 and 2/4 on 1-5. The assist only scales Trace's base speed. It also needs to scale the catch-up speed and the first-gate distance, or offer a real easy mode after 3 fails.
terminal-rush.notes: REMAKE PENDING: the remake (Hacker Dash) scored 7 (needs 8) after 2 rounds this week and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-26 (use that, not the 11-19 branch). Next week: finish it from that branch with the fixes in problems. Remake: type gate words to keep a raccoon ahead of the Trace robot, with jump/duck and fork choices, drones, fire gates, bosses and 36 levels. It looks and plays great for the first 5 levels on both desktop and phone, and the old world-2 wall is mostly gone (an 18 WPM kid now gets about 15 levels in). But the difficulty saw-tooths: new-mechanic levels kill and bosses are breathers. World 5 suddenly needs about 70 WPM, and the chase is rarely tense in a fair way. 7, not shippable yet.

problems: Difficulty curve is inverted at the end: a simple greedy bot lost the Kraken (L6) and barely scratched the Storm Cloud (L12) but beat the final Dragon (L30, 1300 HP) on its first try in 16 moves, because each blocked ! spot deals 18% of max HP. Make the Dragon a real final exam (lower block damage, more spots, shorter bag).

After the goal is met the level keeps going until the bag is empty ('Fill the island for more stars'); let the player bank the win right away with a 'Finish now' button and turn leftover pieces into bonus points.
Catalog title says 'Island Builder' but the title screen says 'Island Town'; Rule 12 says they must match, so update catalog.js.
tile-kingdom.notes: Remade 2026-11-26 (was 3). Remade into a Triple-Town-style hex island merge puzzle (3 huts make a house, chains, goats, rocks, gems, tides, five island bosses) across 30 levels plus endless. It looks great, feels great (CHAIN x3 bursts, confetti, boats and villagers) and adds a new idea every level. Ships at 8, but the final boss needs to be harder.

problems: The difficulty curve sags at the end. A greedy bot with squad level about battle+1 lost The Warlord (battle 12) 3 times in a row, then won Twin Trolls (17) and the final Warlord's Keep (22) on the first try. Bosses from battle 14 on also spawn one level lower. Make the last 4-5 battles at least as hard as battle 12, and don't lower boss levels late.

NEXT always goes straight into the next battle, which is good for pace. But you only reach the ARMY camp from the map or the defeat screen, so a player who only presses Next piles up gold (2,400 unused at battle 9) and hits a wall. Add a small 'Train (gold)' nudge on the victory screen when you can afford a level.

Minor polish: the pause overlay doesn't dim the board, so big floaters like 'DOUBLE KO!' show through behind the PAUSED buttons. With many units, the damage numbers, barks and forecasts stack up and get cluttered.
tiny-tactics.notes: Remade 2026-11-26 (was 3). Remake fixes the earlier problems. Play/Space drops you straight into battle. Enemies scale with your squad: a greedy no-shop bot lost battles 4, 5 and 9 and walled at 9. KO'd units come back HURT at 60% HP. Enemy turns fast-forward and battles take about 25-45 s. Units now have walk/attack/hurt frames, crits get speed-line slow-mo, and there are barks, hidden chests and caged recruits. Works well by mouse and by touch at 390x700. Ships at 8.

problems: Levels 1-1 to 1-4 are the same idea with more trains (5 to 8) and 1-3 switches. My switch-only bot 3-starred all four with big time margins (34/42s, 36/45s, 44/53s, 43/54s) and never needed to brake. The first world needs a twist sooner: introduce braking, a fast express or a paint shed by level 3. The interesting mechanics (river bridges, road crossings, deserts, night) only arrive in world 2+.

The difficulty spike is sharp once the hazards arrive. In 2-5 (bridge + river, 7 switches, 10 trains) and 4-4 (road crossing) the switch-only bot crashed within 7-21s. Tap-the-train braking is never pressed in levels 1-4, so players reach the hard levels without practice. The crash screen is fine, but there is no 'so close!' or replay of what went wrong.

Delivering a train correctly needs a bigger payoff: a bigger chime and confetti burst at the station, a chain multiplier for back-to-back deliveries, and a slow-mo save when two trains just miss each other. Right now success is a small pop and a counter tick. The tutorial is long (about 30s across 6 steps) before the real first level.
junction-jam.notes: Tap switches (or press 1-9) to steer colour-coded toy trains from tunnels to matching stations without crashing, over 60 levels across themed worlds with bridges, road crossings, rivers and night, plus a Rush Hour mode, shop and diorama. A polished, readable, charming diorama look; the best of this batch, held back by a samey first world and modest reward juice.

problems: You aim blind. While you place a well, nothing shows where the marble will go (just a short arrow at the cannon). You press GO, the shot ends in about 1 second, then you guess again. It plays as trial and error, not skill, and the hint button is often the fastest way through.

Winning feels flat. The result is a bare 'GULP!' panel with 3 stars and 3 icon buttons: no count-up, no tease of the next level, no slow-mo as the marble falls in, and the black hole doesn't react. The marble is a plain glowing dot with no character.

Variety is thin and there are no surprises. World 1 (10 levels) is only walls plus 1-2 wells, and there are only 40 levels in total. No critters, golden events or secrets. Bug: if you press GO without re-dragging, the tutorial caption 'Drag it again to fine-tune' stays stuck over the results screen.
gravity-gulp.notes: Physics puzzle: drag attract/repel gravity wells onto the board, press GO, and the cannon's marble curves through stars into a black hole. Four worlds add moving walls, portals plus spikes, and multi-cannon levels. The phone layout rotates well.

problems: build/meta.json still lists 'Hex 2048' / 'Slide hexagon tiles six ways'. The title screen says 'Bee Merge', so the site card describes a different game (Rule 12).
Level 1 is still won in one tap, which is fine as an instant win, but levels 2-4 follow in 5-13 s each, so the first minute passes in a blur of results panels.
On desktop, bosses throw rocks onto the board, but it's easy to miss because the boss sits small in the left panel.
hex-merge.notes: Remade 2026-11-19 (was 2). Tap a honeycomb cell to drop the next honey tile, and 3 or more equal tiles merge and can chain. The fixes landed. It's harder now: the greedy bot lost levels 9 and 21, and a bot playing a random cell 40% of the time lost the bosses at levels 30, 40, 50 and 60 (it still beat level 20). There are 'N moves short of 3 stars' notes, and almost every results screen teases a NEW thing (golden honey, chain-3 HONEY FLOOD, grubs, spreading ice, hornet nests, thief, gusts). Bosses now throw rocks onto the board. It's charming and has one-tap controls. Ships once the meta title and blurb are updated.

problems: The hedges are solid walls with no hint of the way around. A straight-line flier, which is how a kid flies, gets stuck against them. My simple bot dropped from 3 stars to 1 star on days 1-3 and failed the Wasp Queen on day 5, partly from hedge snags plus the spoil timer.
The meadow art is still mostly flat grass with flowers. The bigger scrolling world doesn't have landmarks that make far zones feel like different places.
The spoil countdown number sits right on the bee trail and can be lost among the bees when the trail is long.
hive-mind.notes: Remade 2026-11-19 (was 3). Grab-and-race-home bee-train game. The fixes landed: a scrolling world up to about 1.9x the screen, hedges, a hive pointer with distance, a per-load 'nectar spoils' timer with ticking that speeds up, SPOILED / SO CLOSE feedback, and harder early stars. The phone 🏆 is fixed (opens and stays open). DASH no longer blocks play.

problems: Most puzzles are tiny and solved by just trying directions. BFS optimal solutions: levels 1-4 take 2-4 moves, and levels 11/21/31/41/51 take 4/5/5/6/5. Only level 60 takes 15. Par always equals the optimum, there are no hard spike levels, and 60 levels go by very fast.

The slide feels flat. The penguin glides with a few white specks: no squash or stretch on the bump, no ice-spray trail, no wobble or splash. Reaching a nest is a small chime and the win is a plain white modal (no count-up, no tease of the next level).

No surprises at all: no fish, seals, secrets, idle antics or golden nests. Bug: the tutorial's last step 'Oops? Tap undo' stays over the board and the win modal on later levels until you actually press undo.
ice-slide.notes: Grid ice-sliding puzzle: swipe or arrow keys slide the penguin until it bumps something. Chapters add pushable blocks, holes to fill, heat tiles that melt ice cubes, switches and gates, and several penguins moving at once. Controls are excellent and the art is cute and clean.

problems: The top end is too easy (Rule 11). A 40 WPM bot with 4% typos beats the 5-6 final boss 4/4, and a 50 WPM bot wins every one of the 36 levels 4/4, including 5-6 and R-6, with 2-4 houses left. Fully upgraded, a 30 WPM bot beats the final boss 2/4. A skilled kid will finish the whole game on the first try. Make world 5 and Robot Planet need about 55-65 WPM (faster falls, more meteors on screen at once, an armor or ghost boss phase), and scale the late levels to the upgrades.

Long phrases overlap and can't be read in world 5. On 5-1 at 1280x720 several 30-40 character phrase labels stack on top of each other and over the meteors' faces (for example 'One more meteor and the town is safe!' covering 'hurricane'). One label also sat at the cannon, below the ground line. Make the labels stay out of each other's way (spread phrase meteors across the width, nudge labels apart, or limit how many phrase meteors are on screen at once).

There's no tension for a decent typist for the first 12 levels. 30 WPM and 50 WPM bots lose zero houses in every level of worlds 1 and 2, and the danger only shows up from about 3-2 on. Meanwhile a 10 WPM kid loses 1-3 houses on 1-1 and 1-4 and hits a wall at 2-3 (0/4). Scale the falling speed lightly to the player's measured WPM within a level, so fast kids feel the pressure early and slow kids keep winning in world 1.

Most levels still play the same way. The meteor wave, Final Rush, UFO house rebuild, freeze and bomb chains help, but the screen and the goal never change. Add a few set pieces that change the screen itself (a boss that hides half the sky, a level where the cannon moves, a night level lit only by your shots) so you want to see the next level.
keystorm.notes: REMAKE PENDING: the remake (Meteor Typer) scored 7 (needs 8) after 2 rounds this week and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-26 (use that, not the 11-19 branch). Next week: finish it from that branch with the fixes in problems. Remake: type the word on each falling meteor to blast it and protect six houses, across 36 levels with new meteor types, waves, bosses, Nova and upgrades. The previous notes are really fixed: the curve is now mostly smooth (10 WPM kids clear world 1, 18 WPM reach about 3-3), levels are 12-26 meteors with a Final Rush, explosions are big, and the phone results panel fits. But the endgame falls to a 40-50 WPM typist, long phrases overlap in world 5, and good typists feel no danger for 12 levels. 7, not shippable yet.

problems: Every song plays exactly the same: tap and hold notes on 4 lanes over the same synthwave sun-and-grid backdrop, with only the lane colors and BPM changing. 15 songs bring no new note type, twist, boss song or scene change, so minute 20 feels like minute 2.

Songs run about 100 s and the first song on Easy is sparse (158 notes, roughly 1.5 per second). My first run scored an A at 93.7% with almost no challenge. Each S on Easy is worth 4 stars, so a decent player can unlock most of the list quickly, and on Hard the only difficulty is more notes.

The results screen has only Menu and Retry, with no Next button and no tease of the next song (only a small unlock line). Feedback is generic: a PERFECT pop, a few lane particles and a combo number. There's no hit-stop, no combo milestone fanfare and no reacting crowd or character, so nothing surprising ever happens.
beat-tapper.notes: A 4-lane falling-note rhythm game (DFJK or tap lanes) with procedurally synthesized songs, 3 difficulties, hold notes and S-to-D grades. It's tight and responsive, but you're tapping coloured pills down the same neon highway in every song.

problems: It's far too easy and short. My simple greedy bot (bake, merge the lowest pair, tap to serve) got 3 stars on levels 1-13 without losing a heart. Levels 2-6 lasted 7-27 seconds, and the 6x6 board is never more than a third full, so you're never under pressure.

Levels only change numbers: more customers, a second or third seat, higher tiers, one more flavor. Nothing new mechanically shows up level to level, and level 7 hard-gates you into a text-list shop (Speed, Heat, Patience, Tips, Auto oven) before you can continue.

Merges are weak: a small particle puff and a pop, with screen shake only from tier 6 up. The results card ('Sold out!', stars, +coins, Map/Next) has no count-up and no preview of the next level or customer. Customers are cute static animal heads with almost no reaction.
block-bakery.notes: A merge-and-serve puzzle: tap the oven (or Space) to bake cookies onto a 6x6 grid, drag identical pastries together to tier them up, and tap an item to serve animal customers whose patience bars run down. It looks clean and cute, but it's slow and pressure-free.

problems: The first casts are tiny. The starting line is only 60 m (about 180 px), so the whole dive and reel-up of your first several casts happens on the surface screen in about 3 seconds, and the tutorial's first cast often comes back 'No bite... +0'. The big 'drop deep into the abyss' feeling is gated behind 5+ line upgrades.

Early progress is a slow grind with no burst. My bot earned 6-50 coins per cast against upgrade costs of 20-140, and after 16 casts (about 4 minutes) it had only reached 360 m in the first water. New waters cost 1,200 / 9,000 / 45,000 coins, so a kid sees the same Sunny Shoals fish for a long time.

Catching a fish on the way up is just touching it with the hook: a small +coin float and white sparkle, and small fish are about 20 px at 1280 wide. Jelly stings and the reel-tension minigame (big fish only) are the only drama, the 'MAX DEPTH' toast covers the boat, and there's little juice on landing besides fish flying into the boat.
deep-cast.notes: A Ridiculous-Fishing-style loop: cast, steer the hook down past jellyfish, then hook fish on the way back up, with a hold-to-reel tension minigame for big fish. You sell the catch to upgrade line, hook, lure and boat across 4 waters and 36 species. The art is nice and the loop is solid, but the opening is shallow and slow.

problems: Uneven difficulty between input styles. A fast touch bot got 3 stars on day 1 (919/360) but only 1 star on day 2 (615/510), and a simple zigzag swiper failed day 2 on the phone (397/510). With Playwright mouse input my bots failed day 1 three times (175-229/360). That is partly a test-harness artifact, but day 2 is a sharp wall for a casual swiper.
There is still a lot of the same soil-square grid. The new pond, hay, rocks, trees, sliding rows, tractors and sprinklers break it up, but the core view is the same field screen every day.
The upgrade shop is plain cards with dot bars and only 7 lines. That's fine, but it adds little excitement.
farm-loop.notes: Remade 2026-11-19 (was 2). Fruit-Ninja-style swipe harvester. The fixes landed: the field changes each day (5x3 start, ponds, hay and rocks that break combos, trees, sliding rows), tractor and sprinkler power-ups, chickens that scatter, customers on a market path, tougher stars (1.6x and 2.3x the goal) and bosses. The phone 🏆 is fixed (opens and stays open).

problems: The first league is far beyond a kid. Rookie Row rivals type 36/40/43 WPM, and the first passage has quotes, '#12', '--' and '3/8"'. My 23 WPM 'kid' run placed 4th (last) and only got 'TOP 2 NEEDED'. There's no easy first win, which breaks Rule 1.

The race view is flat: four horizontal dashed lanes with small static car sprites sliding right over a dark band, and the cars have no animation, boost, drafting or reaction to your streaks. The big text box is what you stare at the whole time, so it reads like a typing test with a progress bar.

Progression is the same race repeated: place top 2 twice to move up a league with rivals +10 WPM, 11 times over. Results are a keyboard error heatmap and stats, which are useful but not exciting. There are no streak powers, combo meter or surprise events during the race.
ghost-typer.notes: A typing race: each correct key moves your car along a lane against 3 AI rivals and ghost replays of your best and last runs. You place top 2 twice to climb 11 leagues from 40 to 140 WPM, with an error heatmap and online racing. It's solid for adult typists, but harsh and visually flat for a kid.

problems: Castle 1 (levels 1-10) uses only gems, holes and the gate. The first new idea (rook guards) arrives at level 11, so the first ~10 minutes feel identical. Levels 1-5 are 3-7 forced hops and each one took me 3-7 seconds to clear.

The board is a flat, static checkerboard. Guards never move, tiles have no life, and a hop is a small arc plus a gem pop, with no squash or landing dust. Screen shake fires only on captures and deaths. The castle theme lives on the title screen and barely reaches play.

Nothing surprises you: no secrets, critters, rare events or funny fails. The results panel ('Perfect! 3 stars, Next') has no count-up and no tease of the next level. Tutorial bug: if you keep hopping during 'Undo takes a hop back' and reach the gate, Undo is blocked (the level counts as won), so the tutorial stalls until you press Skip.
knight-quest.notes: Turn-based chess-knight puzzle: tap a glowing square to L-hop, collect every gem, exit through the gate. Later castles add rooks/bishops, walls, crumbling tiles, keys and teleports. Controls are clean (tap, or arrows+Enter, plus undo/hint), but play is a slow, quiet logic puzzle.

problems: Levels 1-3 are one-shot freebies (shoot straight up, par 1); merge them into one opener so the first real bank-shot puzzle arrives in under a minute.
On a 390px phone the board is small with a big empty band under it, and the finger covers the aim point; add an offset/drag-anywhere aim so the thumb sits below the cannon.
Title menu uses three identical white rounded buttons and the desktop side panels (goo tank, zap cells) are static filler; give them lab-themed art and some motion.
laser-lab.notes: Remade 2026-11-26 (was 2). Remade into a bank-shot laser shooter: aim, release, ricochet the beam through goo blobs, mirrors, prisms, portals and bosses across 5 labs/50 levels. Instant, juicy (MEGA combos, golden goo, barrel chains, splats) and late levels need real multi-bounce planning (perfect-aim bot won L39 at par but lost the final boss; naive aiming fails from L10). Ships at 8.

problems: Only the numbers change between levels. All 40 levels are the same timed Boggle board: time drops from 100s to 75s, the target rises from 60 to 1030, the grid grows to 6x6 at level 16 and 4-letter words become required at level 23. Level 40 plays like level 1 with a bigger target.

The difficulty curve is broken. Level 1's 3-star score is 96, which a good player passes about 24 times over (my solver scored 2307 there). Late targets, like 1030 points in 75 seconds with 4-letter minimum words on boards full of Qu, J and X, are out of reach for a 9-year-old who finds 3-4 letter words worth about 5-12 points each.

The dictionary accepts obscure and kid-unsuitable words (GESTAPO, DIKTAT, HIEMAL, INHERED, GENEVAS show up in results). The 'Smash' tiles are rare: bombs spawn on about 3.5% of new tiles, so smashing almost never happens and play stays plain word-spotting.
letter-lattice.notes: Boggle-style word swipe against a timer. Drag through adjacent letter tiles (or type them), score pops up with a combo multiplier, tiles drop in, and 2L/gold/bomb/clock specials unlock over the first levels. The swipe feels good, but every level is the same board chasing a bigger number.

problems: The economy is both too slow and too shallow. My first trips earned $60-240, and refuel plus repair ate $40-70 of that each time, while upgrades start at $150, so early runs feel pointless. Yet there are only 6 upgrades x 5 tiers ($73.8k total), and the 5000+ cash core bonus can buy most of them. That breaks Rule 11's 10+ tiers and hours of progression.

Core play is monotonous. Drilling takes about 0.3-0.5 seconds per tile, and you hold Down through a straight shaft for minutes, inside a small light circle that hides ore. You can't plan routes, and moment to moment, 50m feels the same as 150m. The deeper layers do change colour and add lava, gas, crystals and boulders.

There are no safety cues. The shop lets you leave with low hull and no warning, and my pod died from fall damage seconds after leaving. On the 1280-wide title screen the dirt world stops and the right side is a black void. On phone the 4-way d-pad plus two action buttons cover the bottom third of the screen.
mine-deep.notes: Motherload-style drill pod: drive off the pad, hold arrows to dig down through 6 layers, grab ore, fly back to sell, buy drill/tank/cargo/hull/radar/bomb upgrades, and aim for the core at 1000m. It has the most pull of the five, but it's slow to start and samey within a dive.

problems: The first holes don't hook. Hole 1 is an empty straight lane to the cup, and holes 2-6 add one static bumper, sand, slope or water patch each, with few moving set pieces until the Frost and Neon courses. Most holes are one or two putts and done, and a good aim gets lots of holes-in-one (my solver aced 3 of the first 5).

The feel is thin. A tiny white ball rolls with a faint trail across flat vector shapes. There's no squash, no screen shake on wall hits, no slow-mo on a near-miss lip-out, and no characters or reactive world. The cup is a burst plus a 'HOLE IN ONE!' card. The Neon course is again a plain purple grid with a pink border.

It's short, with little to come back for: 27 holes (about 25 minutes for all of them), and the only long-term pull is ball skins. Visual bug: on hole 1 the tutorial spotlight draws a green/orange diagonal beam from the screen's top-left corner to the ball, on both desktop and phone.
pocket-golf.notes: Top-down minigolf: drag back from the ball and release (or arrows plus Space), with bumpers, sand, slopes, water, ice, spinners and teleporters across 3 nine-hole courses and a scorecard after each hole. It's competent and clear, but flat to look at and quick to finish.

_notes: 2026-11-26: Firebase still not set up, so plays = null. Reviewed 18 never-reviewed games (scores in entries); orbit-defense and tank-duel were also reviewed and picked. Shipped remakes: Laser Bounce, Island Town (renamed from Island Builder), Pocket Army, Spin Defense; tilt-palace bug fix. Not shipped (7s, on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-26): Hacker Dash, Meteor Typer, Tank Wars. Worst still-unremade games for next week: tank-duel/terminal-rush/keystorm WIPs, then score 3s from 11-19 (pocket-golf, block-bakery, knight-quest, beat-tapper, letter-lattice, ghost-typer), then 4s (gale-regatta, asteroid-miner, bounce-brigade, ember-drift, neon-serpent, sky-hopper, gravity-gulp, rune-match, deep-cast, ice-slide). Never reviewed yet: zombie-fort, moto-hill, boing-voyage, kickflip-alley, canopy-swing, wreckaroo, slingstar, springflip-circus, knuckle-comet, pinquake + the 11-13 batch.

problems: You can't lose early: the ball save switches back on every time it saves a ball, so any ball that drains within about 10 seconds of launch comes back forever. In my no-flipper AFK test, ball 1 lasted 150+ seconds and the game never ended. The tutorial's 'Shift nudges' step also has no timeout, and its 999-second ball save stays on until the player presses Shift.

Too easy and too short (Rule 11): a crude 'flip when the ball is near' bot kept one ball alive for minutes and scored 11M on Crown Jewel, while the next table unlocks at 2M. You can open the next table in your first game, and nothing on the table pushes back.

The six tables are basically reskins. Crown Jewel, Volcano Temple and Clockwork Dragon all have the same flippers, slings, twin ramps, lane row and mission-icon ring, with only colours, the boss toy and bumper spots changed. Missions are tiny icons with no clear 'shoot HERE' goal, and after about 3 minutes of play only one mission had been completed.
tilt-palace.notes: A glossy, phone-friendly pinball game with a dot-matrix display, multiball and a reacting boss helmet. It looks and feels like a real table in the first minute. But it's far too forgiving, and the 'new' tables don't play differently enough to pull you forward. Suggested blurb: Flip, smash bumpers and wake the boss on six wild tables. 2026-11-26: bug fix shipped (ball save no longer re-arms forever; shooter-lane softlock and tutorial timeouts fixed). Still a remake candidate (score 5).

problems: Way too easy (Rule 11). A slow bot that cooks one order at a time and waits for every pot got 3 stars, all PERFECT and 0 angry customers on Days 1, 2, 3, 7 (cat) and 8 (critic + rush + rain), with zero upgrades bought. There's no rush in Ramen Rush: patience is so long that you never have to juggle two pots or plan ahead.

Early shifts have dead time. On Days 1-2 the counter sat empty for 15-30 seconds at a stretch between customers, so the 100-second shift is half waiting. With only one pot, each bowl is also a fixed 5-second wait while the noodles boil.

Every bowl is the same chain of 5-7 separate drags (bin, pot, tray, broth, topping, board swipe, tray, customer) across 12+ stations. It feels like chores rather than one great action. Order bubbles are small pictures where toppings and chili are hard to read, especially on a phone. The results card has no tease of what the next day brings.
noodle-rush.notes: A night-market ramen stall cooking game with lovely illustrated customers, steam, a cat and big PERFECT combo bursts. It looks and feels polished, but there's no pressure at all, so the 'rush' never comes and the days blur together. Suggested blurb: Boil, slice and slurp-serve ramen before the queue explodes!

problems: The controls are realistic sailing homework, not a 5-second game. You steer, trim the sail and tack (three inputs, plus a slider on phone), and turning anywhere near the wind drops you to 0.0 kn with 'In irons! Bear away'. My steering bot, using the same tack-at-an-angle logic as the AI, kept stalling in irons and once sat stuck against a rock for minutes. A 9-year-old will hit this constantly.

Losing feels unfair and blocks progress. On Harbour race 1 (Windward Dash) the AI boats finished in 1:19-1:37, while my bot came 6th of 6 twice (1:52 and much worse). Race 2 and every other venue stay locked until you podium, so a struggling kid replays the same first race forever.

The first seconds are a tiny boat on a big empty blue sea. The boat takes up about 3% of the screen, there's nothing to hit or collect near the start, and the first thing the tutorial teaches is how to not stall. The results card also has a big blank area above the time when you don't medal.
gale-regatta.notes: A top-down sailboat race against five AI rivals, with real wind, tacking and sail trim. It looks clean and calm, but the realistic no-go-zone sailing is confusing and punishing for a kid, so it's slow to get fun and easy to get stuck at the back. Suggested blurb: Catch the wind, slingshot the buoys, beat five rival boats!

problems: The water is too small to be satisfying. The flow is a thin trickle of a few pixels running along the very top of a huge dirt cross-section, and roughly 80% of the board (all the buried rocks, sand, worms and clay) is just decoration that you never dig into. The core 'guide real water' moment has no splash or rush and gives almost no feedback until a small 'Bloom!' at the end.

The levels repeat themselves. Meadow 1-6 and Volcano 1-3 were all the same task: scrape a shallow ditch along the surface from the spring to 1-3 plants or critters, press the water button, wait 15-40 seconds. Volcano mostly changes the colours plus a lava pocket, and no level I played needed a pipe, gate or any real thinking.

It's too easy and too small on a phone. Following the obvious route gave 3 stars on every level I tried (9 of 9), and you mostly wait while the water creeps along. At 390x700 the whole diorama is a 250px strip, so a finger channel only a few pixels wide is fiddly, and the GB gear tab covers the goal icons at the top.
trickle-valley.notes: A water-digging puzzle on a hillside cross-section, with sprouts, ducks and frogs to water. It has a cozy look and simple drag-to-dig controls, but the water is tiny and slow and the levels play the same, so it feels more like a calm toy than a game you can't put down. Suggested blurb: Dig a ditch, unleash the water, and wake the thirsty frogs!

problems: The animals look stiff and AI-made up close, which matters because zooming in on them IS the game. The rolling 'dust bath' zebra is a jumbled tangle of rotated body parts, the gazelle has a see-through white blob on its body and a lumpy double head, and background zebras have bullseye-ring stripes on their rumps. In dust-storm weather the whole screen turns one muddy brown.

There's too much dead time on the jeep ride. Long stretches of the Savanna tour have zero animals on screen (empty ground and bushes), and with only 10-12 film shots and a slow auto-drive you spend a lot of the 3-minute tour just waiting. Holding S to stop also takes over a second to bite.

Great shots are too cheap to feel special. My very first unaimed tap on a phone gave a 4-star 'LEGENDARY · With baby' print worth 637, and a 1-star cut-off photo was also labelled LEGENDARY. When the rare tag pops up for sloppy shots, the 'wait for the perfect moment' tension that should drive the game disappears.
wild-lens.notes: A safari photo game where you ride a jeep, aim a viewfinder, zoom and snap animals into an album, with a nice camp/region map and polaroid prints. The core snap-and-print loop is pleasant, but the animal art doesn't hold up when zoomed, tours have empty stretches, and 'legendary' shots come too easily to hook you. Suggested blurb: Zoom, wait, SNAP! Catch wild animals doing silly things.

problems: Too much waiting between shots: every round stops for rival volleys and a scoreboard panel, and the tutorial takes 4 shots plus text bubbles, so you spend more time watching than shooting. Cut rival volleys to one quick animation and let a tap skip everything.

Each shot takes several steps (drag down, wait for full-draw lock, drag again to aim, hold Shift or the Steady button, release). On a phone, steadying needs a second finger on the Steady button while the first finger drags. Make steadying automatic while you hold still at full draw, or put it on the same finger.

The reticle shows where you aim, not where the arrow will land, so at 70-90 m with wind you have to guess the drop. That is real skill, but there is no assist or landing-ghost preview for kids. The crowd is static coloured capsule people, which looks cheap and AI-made next to the nicely animated archer.
quiver-peak.notes: An over-the-shoulder archery career (6 tournaments, challenges, storm range) with nice painterly alpine art. Hitting a 10 feels good, but the pace is slow and step-heavy, so it isn't a 'can't put it down' game yet. Note: it ran at only about 4 fps in the headless test box, so smoothness was not judged.

problems: You can't fail. A bot that never presses anything still finishes every one of the 12 tracks and gets bronze, and police 'BUSTED' only slows you down. Missed grabs need real stakes (spin-out, fall in the creek, a timer or a caught-by-police end).

It's too short for Rule 11: 12 tracks of 4-40 s each is about 6 minutes of content. Gold (bot-perfect time x1.05) is the only real challenge, and the 8 paints unlock quickly from stars. It needs more tracks or worlds, a harder tier or mirror mode, and longer-term unlocks.
On a phone, the gb settings tab sits right on top of the big centre timer. Level 1 'First Bend' is a 3.6 s straight-bend-straight that ends almost before it begins.
tetherdrift.notes: A one-button top-down drift racer: hold to rope a corner post, release to sling out. The rope swing, PERFECT pops, combos, cows and the toy-diorama look are genuinely satisfying. It is let down by having no fail state and too little content.

problems: The player does almost nothing: one tap per level, then 10-30 s of watching. When you miss by 1 ('So close! 15/16' three times in a row on Wind Gust), it feels like luck rather than skill, because the preview ring only shows first-hop hits, not the full chain. Give more agency, for example the mid-chain spark taps on every level, or a full-chain preview line.

Every level is the same screen full of near-identical smiling lanterns over the same river town. New lantern types are small icons in a crowd, so level 8 looks like level 1. The scene, time of night, weather or layout shapes need to change so each level looks different.

Some goals are calibrated from a grid of random taps and land just above what an obvious 'tap the big cluster' shot gives (Big Lantern needs 16; tapping the obvious cluster gave 11). Kids will retry the same tap and fail with no idea why. On a phone, the gb settings tab covers the GOAL/chain readout.
glowburst.notes: A one-tap chain-reaction fireworks puzzle at a lantern festival. Big chains look and sound lovely, especially on a phone, but with one tap and then watching it's too passive to hold Charlie for long.

problems: The Big Wiggler boss (level 15) is a wall. A sloppy bot was gulped within 5-9 s, and even the game's own smart bot failed it 2 out of 2 times at 18-28 s, right after easy levels where nothing could kill you. The boss needs a fairer ramp (a slower start, a warning, or checkpoints) or a softer lead-in level.
Floating texts pile on top of each other and become unreadable: 'WORM CHAIN x8!' overlaps '+1', and 'SPLASH!' sits under 'PERFECT!' and 'x2'. Stack or queue the pops so the big moments read clearly.

On a phone (portrait), you can only see a short way ahead, so rocks and lava come too fast to react to. The gb settings tab also covers the level progress bar. Pull the camera out or lead it further in the direction of travel when in portrait.
burrow-bolt.notes: A one-button mole dive-and-leap momentum game. Hold to dig, release to burst out, gulp worm arcs. It is juicy, with painterly cross-section art and a new hazard every level (rocks, rabbits, fox, water, lava, boss). It is close to shipping, held back by the boss spike and messy text pops.

problems: The early game is far too easy. The perfect window is large (+6/+3 bonus on levels 1-2) and a magnet pulls the falling animal onto the stack, so dropping anywhere near the middle scores perfect after perfect (the bot got 10/10 perfects on level 3). There's no tension until about level 10.

The feel is soft. A perfect is a small 'PERFECT!' text and a ding, with no hit-stop, shake or big burst, and the tower barely wobbles until it suddenly topples. Make the lean and sway readable and scary, and make perfects louder.
On a phone, the gb settings tab covers the centre combo counter. The results screen gave '+0' coins on a 1-star clear, which feels like no reward.
teeter-zoo.notes: A crane-drop animal stacking game (Tower Bloxx style) with charming soft vector animals, a new animal or base twist every level, and 30 levels plus endless. It's pretty and easy to pick up, but too forgiving early and not punchy enough to be a must-play. Suggested blurb: Stack squishy zoo animals sky-high before the tower topples!

problems: The early songs are too easy (Rule 11). Windows are wide (about ±60 ms for Perfect and ±120 ms for Good), and a bot with ±40 ms random timing error 3-starred Cymbal Sky (3 misses) and Bird Song (1 miss in 69). Sunny Kick and Bongo Bounce were 2-star with 7-8 misses. The health bar never came close to emptying.

The first 4-5 songs all use the same sunny jungle and the same red drums. Each new idea (double time, logs, cymbals) is only a different drum on an identical scene, so the 'new place' feeling only arrives at world 2 (dusk festival lake).

Surprise moments are thin: background critters bob and there is an occasional golden drum, but nothing unexpected happens in the middle of a song. On a 390x700 phone the gb settings tab sits on top of the song progress bar.
drumhop.notes: Rhythm one-button game: the ball auto-hops across drums and you tap as it lands, with long hold drums, cymbal launches, a call-and-response bird and a toad boss. It has the best looks and controls of my batch and results screens that tease the next song, but early songs are too forgiving to feel thrilling.

problems: Far too easy (Rule 11). A bot that just uses the game's own rival AI (botInput, skill 1) won 1st place and gold on all 4 Ash Canyon tracks on the first try, 3-4 s under gold each time (e.g. 45.3 s vs a 48.6 s gold). Rivals use that same AI, slowed down by pace multipliers, so they can never press a good player.

Most of the screen is an empty dark-brown void with a few rocks and orange shards. The car is tiny, there is no scenery or landmarks, and all 4 tracks in a cup look the same. The trophy and some UI icons are emoji.
Results only show medals and a time, with no peek at what the next track adds. New ideas (ice, boost pads, geysers) are subtle and easy to miss, so track 4 feels like track 1.
ember-drift.notes: Top-down drift racer: hold to drift, build the ember meter, release to boost, race 3 AI cars over 12 tracks. The drift-chain-boost juice ('SUPER!', chain x5) is good, but it is too easy and visually empty. Suggested blurb: Hold to drift, let go to rocket past your rivals!

problems: It looks exactly like the generic AI neon look Charlie dislikes: glowing lines and dots on a black grid, with no world, character or lighting. The snake is a glowing tube with two dots for eyes.

The core action is plain grid Snake. Portals, fever and 'CLOSE!' shaves are bolted on, but turning at 90 degrees on a grid feels the same at stage 3 as at stage 1. My BFS bot 3-starred stages 1-2 first try and cleared stage 3 on its second attempt, so the early campaign has little tension. Stage 20 (spiral, crates, movers) is the first place where it really died.
The results screen has stars and a score but no tease of the next stage. On a 390x700 phone the score at the top is covered by the gb settings tab and the red timer ring.
neon-serpent.notes: Grid snake with portals, fever combos, power-ups and a 24-stage campaign. Controls are clean and instant, but it is a classic idea in a flat neon-on-black skin, so Charlie would call it 'kind of just simple'. Suggested blurb: Warp through portals and grow the longest snake ever!

problems: It plays like a plain Doodle-Jump tower: flat green bars, coins and a small blob. Biomes every 200 m are mostly a palette swap, so minute 5 feels like minute 1. On desktop the 420 px tower is a thin strip in the middle of a 1280 px screen, with empty sky on both sides.

Progression is short (Rule 11). There are only 5 upgrades with 2-3 tiers each (about 10k coins in total), plus skins. There are no levels or goals besides beating your height, and the game-over screen has no tease.

Controls use 4 inputs (left, right, jump, dash), and the phone has 4 small on-screen buttons. During the desktop tutorial a long blue diagonal beam runs from the top-left corner to the player and looks like a rendering bug. My simple bot died to the lava at 15-128 m, so the lava does push, but deaths come from slow climbing rather than exciting near-misses.
sky-hopper.notes: Endless vertical climber with wall-jumps, run-speed super jumps and rising lava. It is competent and responsive but generic, and there is little new to see or unlock.

problems: Play opens the upgrade shop instead of the game, and a first-timer then goes through a 5-caption tutorial, so the first 10 seconds are menus and reading, not blasting.

Sectors are long and samey: each one is 3 waves plus a boss (2+ minutes), the space backdrop looks the same every sector, and the only new thing is one extra enemy type. The sector 1 boss is a spinning hexagon with 1100 HP that takes close to a minute of holding fire with the starting blaster.

It's a twin-stick shooter with manual mouse aim, and on phone you need both thumbs on two sticks. There is no auto-aim (Rule 3 says the shooter should aim for you). Enemies are plain pink triangles and circles and the rocks are flat purple blobs, so it reads as generic and AI-made.
asteroid-miner.notes: Top-down twin-stick asteroid shooter with ore, upgrades and 10 sectors with bosses. It's competent and works, but it feels flat and the same from sector to sector. My bot died on the S1 boss without upgrades, so it isn't too easy. Suggested blurb: Shred asteroids, vacuum up ore, outgun ten giant space bosses

problems: Stages drag: my ball-tracking bot needed 143 seconds to clear stage 1-1 (24 bricks). The ball often loops with nothing to hit, and the last few bricks take forever (Rule 2 wants 20-90 s).

It looks like stock breakout: flat rounded rectangles in rows on a purple gradient, in a narrow column with big empty sides on desktop. Later worlds just recolour the same layout, and the 'boss' is a rectangle with googly eyes.

Brick breaks are weak (small burst, no hit-stop, no real screen shake) and there are no surprises. The pick-1-of-3 cards are the only new thing between stages, so nothing makes you want to see the next stage.
bounce-brigade.notes: A brick breaker roguelite with upgrade cards, 5 worlds and bosses. It plays fine, but it's a plain breakout clone that is slow to finish a stage and looks the same everywhere. Suggested blurb: Smash bricks, grab crazy power-ups, crush the googly-eyed bosses

problems: It's too easy and too short (Rule 11). The dotted arc preview makes most shots free, and a bot with ±14 px random error got 2-3 stars on 10 of 11 levels in about 3 minutes, so the 30-level career is roughly a 10-minute game.

Every career level uses the same flat park court and the same static shooter. Courts only change if you buy them in the shop, so the new twists (bank, wind, wall, moving hoop) don't feel like new places.
A made basket gives only a small 'SWISH!' word and a little confetti. There's no slow-mo, net snap, crowd, streak fire or hit-stop, so a great shot doesn't feel amazing.
hoop-shot.notes: A side-view drag-back basketball game with 30 short twist levels. It has the best hook and controls of this batch, but it's shallow, easy and visually plain.

problems: The dash-slash, which is supposed to be the hook, has little impact: the enemy just vanishes in a few dark pixels with a small 'SLICE +3'. There's no hit-stop, no split-in-half body, no big sparks or shake, so killing doesn't feel great.
On the 390x700 phone the camera keeps the ninja at the left with only about 270 px of world ahead at 330+ px/s (under 1 s to react), so gaps and spikes arrive too fast to read. Desktop is fine.

The first tutorial stage is an endless run that waits for each action (about 45 s before the real stage 1). Region bosses are simple shapes (the bamboo boss is a red ball with horns), and stages within a region reuse the same chunks, so it gets samey after a few stages.
dash-ninja.notes: An auto-runner ninja with jump and dash-slash across 4 good-looking regions (bamboo, sakura, night castle) and bosses. It's the most polished of these five, but the core slash lacks punch and the levels repeat.

problems: Holding one key is punished now but can still get through world 1 with retries. A bot that only held Right took heavy damage (57/100 HP on wave 1), overheated, and lost waves 6 and 7 three times in total, but retrying the wave let it reach wave 7. It is no longer free, but a kid who mashes can still grind through Candy Cove.

The wave-clear sequence takes about 1.2 s before the cards show up. The 'WAVE CLEAR!' letters drop in from the upper left over the whale, and 'Pick one!' with no cards visible looks like an empty screen for a moment. Bring the cards in sooner.
The phone tutorial says 'Drag around to spin!', but holding either half of the screen also works and is easier. The hint could show the hold-left/right zones so players aren't misled.
orbit-defense.notes: Remade 2026-11-26 (was 3). Remake check: the wave soft-lock is fixed. 'THEY CHARGE!' rage kicks in, so a 5-gun Void wave 3 cleared in about 41 s, and a weak 1-gun build ended with a loss in about 12-37 s instead of stalling. World 1 now has overheat, shells and a bomber wave 7 that killed the aim bot once from full HP. Headings are now multicolour sticker text ('PERFECT!', 'WAVE 1 CLEAR!') with confetti and stars. Played world 1 and world 2 waves 1-5 on desktop and world 1 waves 1-5 with touch at 390x700. No errors. Ships.

problems: Duel 14 (Moon Twins: low gravity plus two enemies) is still a wall. A good-human bot (small aim error that shrinks with each shot) lost 6 out of 6 with gear 6 and with gear 8 (172+ HP). It often left both enemies near full HP after only 3-6 shots. A near-perfect bot went 1 for 2 at gear 6. Two enemies firing every round in low gravity drains you too fast. Give twin duels less AI accuracy or less HP, or let only one twin fire per round.

Duel 20 (Iron King) feels unfair, not just hard. Even a near-perfect bot at gear 9 lost 3 out of 3, twice dying after only 2 shots in 21-26 s (208 HP gone in two enemy rounds). The boss's double shell plus a second tank deletes the player before they can aim. Cap damage per enemy round, or give the boss its second shell only every other turn.

Small issues: headings like 'DIRECT HIT!' and the twist banner ('Low gravity! + Two enemies!') are still a plain heavy sans with an outline, unlike the gradient 'VICTORY!'. In the 390x700 online match the player's own tank sits partly behind the SHELL weapon button at bottom-left.
tank-duel.notes: REMAKE PENDING: the remake (Tank Wars) scored 7 (needs 8) after 2 rounds this week and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-26 (use that, not the 11-19 branch). Next week: finish it from that branch with the fixes in problems. Remake check: duel 10 Big Bertha is fixed. At gear 4 the bot lost once (boss left at 42 HP) and then won, and duel 11 went the same way. Impacts are much better: large craters, chunky dirt spray, a bigger damage number and the camera follows the shell. Looks are much better too: trees, cacti, crystals, birds, layered dirt, tanks with treads and drivers. Played duels 1-6 on desktop, 1-4 by touch with the tutorial, plus 10-12, 14-15 and 20. 'Battle Online' then 'Play vs bots' starts a 4-tank match right away, and my shots registered (one hit for 42). Duels 14 and 20 still wall a good player, so it holds at 7.
